title: Peak Watch
statement: A river gauge records one water level per hour in readings. Flood monitors watch a rolling window of the latest k hours. For every window of k consecutive readings, from the first window to the last, report the highest reading inside it. Return those maxima in order.

examples.explanation: Windows of size 1 report each reading.

hints.content: Taking the max of every window separately costs k per window.
A reading that is followed by a higher reading can never again be a window's maximum.
Keep candidate indices in a double-ended queue whose readings strictly decrease from front to back.
Before adding index i, pop indices from the back whose readings are <= readings[i]. Drop the front index once it falls out of the window.
Once i >= k - 1, the front of the deque is the index of the current window's maximum.

testCases.explanation: Windows of size 1 report each reading.
Rising levels: each window's max is its right end.
Falling levels: each window's max is its left end.

solutions.title: Scan every window
solutions.approach: For each start s from 0 to n - k, take the maximum of readings[s..s+k-1].
commonMistakes: Producing n windows instead of n - k + 1.
Starting best at 0, which fails for all-negative windows.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Each window is scanned on its own, so the cost is O(n·k), up to 10^8 when k is around n/2.

solutions.title: Monotonic deque of indices
solutions.intuition: Older readings that are not larger than a newer one are useless; the survivors form a decreasing sequence whose front is the maximum.
solutions.approach: Keep a deque (an array with a moving head) of indices with strictly decreasing readings. For each i: pop smaller-or-equal readings from the back, push i, advance the head if it is outside the window, and after the first full window record the reading at the head.
solutions.pseudocode:
dq = []
for i: while dq and r[dq.back] <= r[i]: pop back
  push i; if dq.front <= i - k: pop front
  if i >= k - 1: out.push(r[dq.front])
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n) beyond the output; expired indices remain before the moving head
commonMistakes: Storing values instead of indices, which makes expiry impossible to detect.
Using shift() for the front on a large array, which can make the loop quadratic; a moving head index avoids that.
solutions.interviewExplanation: I keep a deque of indices whose readings strictly decrease. A new reading evicts everything not larger than it from the back, because those can never be a maximum again. The front leaves when it falls out of the window. The front is always the current maximum, and every index enters and leaves once, so it's O(n). I use a head pointer instead of shift() to keep pops constant time.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: i=3 adds -3: [1,2,3]; record 3. i=4 (5) evicts everything: [4]; record 5.
